forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Tamworth took out no new loans in 2025/26 despite £17.2m of capital spending
news_drafts.lead:
Tamworth Borough Council took out no new loans in 2025/26, even though it spent £17.2m on capital spending (money spent on things that last, such as buildings and equipment). The figure is in the annual treasury management report (how the council borrows and invests its cash) that went to its Audit and Governance Committee on 24 September 2026.

The council's total borrowing stayed at £63.060m, unchanged from the year before. The report says the spending was paid for from the council's own cash and from capital receipts (money from asset sales), a practice known as internal borrowing. This saves interest but uses up the council's cash cushion. The report puts the gap between what the council has borrowed and what its capital spending would otherwise require at £7.158m, which it describes as an under-borrowed position.

The council says the reason was cost. In the report's words: "Due to the elevated cost of borrowing long-term, no borrowing was undertaken during the year." The papers describe the approach as a continuing strategy, not a one-year decision.
news_drafts.paper_title: Annual Report on the Treasury Management Service and Actual Prudential Indicators 2025/26 enc. 1

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Mid-year Review 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Tamworth says its treasury position will support the move to any new unitary arrangements from the strongest possible financial position
findings.detail: The paper links treasury operations and cash flow planning to the Financial Resilience Plan and to local government reorganisation. It says there are no direct reorganisation implications in the recommendations.
findings.matters: Councils in reorganisation areas are being asked to show how their treasury and cash planning will carry into any new unitary body, which is relevant to other councils facing the same change.
findings.quote: ensuring that it enters any new unitary arrangements from the strongest possible financial position

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Mid-year Review 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Tamworth has £40m in eight £5m deposits with other councils, the highest at 5.11% to Blackpool City Council
findings.detail: Appendix 1 lists deposits with Gloucester, Bradford, Medway, Lancashire, West Northamptonshire, Newham, Moray and Blackpool, with rates from 4.35% to 5.11%. Three money market funds make up the remaining £11.557m.
findings.matters: A council that lends to other councils is also a counterparty to them, so the rates and terms it accepts show what peer councils are paying for short-term cash.
findings.figures: Eight deposits of £5,000,000 each (£40m total); Blackpool City Council rate 5.11%; Newham and Moray 4.80%; money market funds £11.557m

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Mid-year Review 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Tamworth's property fund valuation was £6.699m at 30 September 2026, an overall loss of £1.207m since the 2022 gain
findings.detail: The paper says the funds recovered after 2020 and gained £1.132m by March 2022 before falling again. The paper also reports £86,537 in dividends from the funds to 30 September 2026, which it says is part of the 2026/27 revenue budget; the text separately gives £276k for 2026/27 and £442k for 2025/26. The paper says the Hermes fund is no longer held.
findings.matters: Property fund losses reduce the capital value of a council's treasury holdings and the dividends that support its revenue budget, which is a risk other councils holding similar funds will want to measure.
findings.figures: Valuation £6.699m at 30 September 2026; overall loss £1.207m; dividends £86,537 to 30 September 2026; 2026/27 dividends £276k (text); 2025/26 dividends £442k; 2026/27 year-to-date return -1.3%
findings.quote: as at 30 th September the valuation stands at £6.699m, with an overall loss of £1.207m

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Mid-year Review 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: No debt has been repaid or rescheduled in 2026/27 to date, although the paper says repayment and rescheduling opportunities have increased
findings.detail: The paper says debt repayment and rescheduling will be considered where they give long-term savings. No action has been taken so far this financial year.
findings.matters: Rising opportunities to restructure debt, with none yet taken, is a position a lender or peer finance team would want to track as rates move.
findings.figures: Gross borrowing £63.060m (no repayments or rescheduling to date)
findings.quote: no debt repayments or rescheduling has been undertaken to date in the current financial year.

findings.paper_title: Annual Investment Strategy Mid-year Review 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Tamworth plans no additional borrowing in 2026/27 and will use £15.94m of cash flow funds in place of borrowing against £63.060m of existing borrowing
findings.detail: The paper calls the internal borrowing approach prudent and cost effective in the current climate, but says it will need monitoring if gilt yields stay high at the long end of the curve.
findings.matters: A council choosing to use its own cash rather than new borrowing while gilt yields are elevated is a decision other finance directors may be weighing for themselves.
findings.figures: Gross borrowing £63.060m; cash flow funds used in lieu of borrowing £15.94m; revised CFR £79.00m
findings.quote: It is not anticipated that any additional borrowing will be undertaken during 2026/27.
